questions.explain: TDE encrypts data/log/backup files at rest but decrypts transparently at the storage layer — a rogue DBA running SELECT * FROM dbo.CreditCards gets plaintext every time. It offers no protection against compromised logins or privileged users.
options: Data at rest on stolen storage media
Data in memory from a compromised DBA account
Backup files from being read
Data files from offline theft
questions.q: What does TDE NOT protect against, per the chapter?

questions.explain: The chapter's production gotcha: if the SQL Server managed identity loses Key Vault access, the server goes into an inaccessible state within minutes — no queries, no restores — until access is restored. Alert on Key Vault access failures.
options: The database automatically falls back to a service-managed key
Backups continue working normally
The server becomes inaccessible within minutes — no queries, no restores — until Key Vault access is restored
TDE encryption pauses until access returns
questions.q: What happens if the SQL Server managed identity loses access to Key Vault when using customer-managed TDE keys?

questions.explain: Deterministic encryption produces the same ciphertext for the same plaintext, supporting equality predicates (WHERE SSN = @ssn). Randomized is more secure but supports no predicates — select only by returning the column.
options: Deterministic uses stronger keys
Deterministic supports equality comparisons (WHERE SSN = @ssn); randomized supports no predicates
Randomized supports range queries
Both support LIKE pattern matching
questions.q: What is the practical difference between deterministic and randomized Always Encrypted column encryption?

questions.explain: Ledger maintains a SHA-256 hash tree (Merkle-tree-like) over table rows: each transaction produces a block with a hash of changed rows plus the previous block's hash. Modifying any historical row invalidates all subsequent hashes, and sp_verify_database_ledger recomputes the chain.
options: By encrypting the history table
By requiring two-phase commits
By replicating rows to Azure Confidential Ledger
By maintaining a SHA-256 hash tree over rows, where each block chains to the previous block's hash
questions.q: How does Azure SQL Ledger make data tamper-evident?

questions.explain: The chapter's layering summary: TDE protects against stolen storage media, Always Encrypted protects against privileged DBAs/compromised credentials, and Ledger protects against tampering with historical data — none substitutes for the others.
options: TDE replaces the other two
Always Encrypted replaces TDE for backups
TDE stops storage theft, Always Encrypted stops privileged-user data exposure, Ledger makes tampering provable
Ledger encrypts columns so Always Encrypted is redundant
questions.q: How do TDE, Always Encrypted, and Ledger combine as defense in depth, per the chapter?
